name: Bench press
angleNote: Bar height: 0% = on the chest, 100% = arms locked out. Torques are per arm; drag the figure to turn it.
momentArmNote: Moment arm = the joint's 3D distance from the bar's push line through that hand; it feeds every component of that joint's torque.

joints.name: Shoulder (across)
joints.angleLabel: upper-arm angle (0° = out to the side, 90° = up)

strength.note: Relative horizontal-adduction strength vs arm angle (0° = arms out in line with the shoulders): constant from 30° behind that line to 60° in front, then a sharp drop (Williams & Stutzman, 10 men; Whitley, 31 men, found no change over 60°; both via Kulig et al.). How far it drops by 90–120° isn't given numerically, so those values are estimates. Peak per arm is still an estimate (TODO).
strength.source: Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shape; drop beyond 60° and peak torque estimated)

strength.note: Shoulder flexion (positive) and extension (negative) peak torque per arm, taken as constant across the range: Mayer's isometric means for men (68 and 93 Nm), measured standing.
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric)

strength.note: Shoulder external (positive) and internal (negative) rotation peak torque per arm, taken as constant: Mayer's isometric means for men (30 and 43 Nm).
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric)

strength.note: Relative isometric elbow-extension torque vs elbow flexion (0° = straight), peak about 55°: the paper's mean cubic fit, normalised, inside the measured 20–116° (held flat beyond). Measured with the upper arm raised 90° to the side, so the long head's length differs from overhead or arm-at-side positions. Peak per arm: the paper's male mean, 77 Nm (rounded to 80 for trained lifters).
strength.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001

strength.note: No muscle capacity: the elbow's sideways moment is carried mostly by ligaments and the joint surfaces, so it is shown as torque only.
strength.source: Not applicable: carried by ligaments and joint surfaces, so no muscle strength is used

muscles.name: Pectoralis major
muscles.note: Main horizontal adductor. Measured: wider grips raise the shoulder's moment and the abdominal head's EMG; the sternocostal head barely changes (Mausehund et al.).
muscles.source: Activation weights: TODO. Grip-width effect: Mausehund L, Werkhausen A, Bartsch J, Krosshaug T (2022). Understanding bench press biomechanics — the necessity of measuring lateral barbell forces. J Strength Cond Res 36(10):2685–2695

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Shoulder flexor; also helps horizontal adduction.

muscles.name: Triceps
muscles.note: Elbow extensor. Measured: narrower grips raise the elbow's moment (by up to 26%) and the lateral head's EMG (Mausehund et al.). This model's elbow moment arm (15–20 cm) is about twice the measured one (7–9 cm), so its triceps numbers run high.
muscles.source: Activation weights: TODO. Grip-width effect and moment arms: Mausehund L, Werkhausen A, Bartsch J, Krosshaug T (2022). Understanding bench press biomechanics — the necessity of measuring lateral barbell forces. J Strength Cond Res 36(10):2685–2695

muscles.name: Infraspinatus, teres minor
muscles.note: External rotators of the rotator cuff: hold the upper arm from turning inwards.

muscles.name: Subscapularis
muscles.note: Internal rotator of the rotator cuff: holds the upper arm from turning outwards.

phases.name: Off the chest
phases.text: Bar on the chest, furthest in front of the shoulder: the shoulder's largest moment arm.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: The bar moves back over the shoulder as it rises.

phases.name: Lockout
phases.text: Bar over the shoulders: little shoulder torque; whatever the elbows still do depends on the grip.

variants.name: Flat bench, medium grip
variants.notes: Hands about 1.7× shoulder width, elbows stacked under the hands in the front view. The flare angle follows from the arm's geometry (shown under the table). Each hand pushes up with half the bar; how hard the hands pull the bar apart (or squeeze it) can't be found from statics, so by default they don't. Lifters do pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow, and the least-effort option predicts similar values (26%, 41%, 2%). With those forces this model's elbow torques move the wrong way, because its elbow placement and fixed shoulders don't match real pressing, so the default stays at zero. The shoulder joints stay put; real shoulder blades move, so the mid-press elbow numbers are probably on the high side.

variants.name: Wide grip
variants.notes: Hands far out: the upper arms flare, the pecs (horizontal adduction) work much harder and the triceps much less. The bar also travels less. Each hand pushes up with half the bar; how hard the hands pull the bar apart (or squeeze it) can't be found from statics, so by default they don't. Lifters do pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow, and the least-effort option predicts similar values (26%, 41%, 2%). With those forces this model's elbow torques move the wrong way, because its elbow placement and fixed shoulders don't match real pressing, so the default stays at zero. The shoulder joints stay put; real shoulder blades move, so the mid-press elbow numbers are probably on the high side.

variants.name: Close grip
variants.notes: Hands at shoulder width, elbows tucked: the triceps take over and the pecs' across-the-body work nearly vanishes. Each hand pushes up with half the bar; how hard the hands pull the bar apart (or squeeze it) can't be found from statics, so by default they don't. Lifters do pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow, and the least-effort option predicts similar values (26%, 41%, 2%). With those forces this model's elbow torques move the wrong way, because its elbow placement and fixed shoulders don't match real pressing, so the default stays at zero. The shoulder joints stay put; real shoulder blades move, so the mid-press elbow numbers are probably on the high side.

variants.name: Medium grip, elbows flared past the hands
variants.notes: Elbows pushed 6 cm outside the hands and the bar lowered higher on the chest: see how the rotation torque and flare angle change. Each hand pushes up with half the bar; how hard the hands pull the bar apart (or squeeze it) can't be found from statics, so by default they don't. Lifters do pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow, and the least-effort option predicts similar values (26%, 41%, 2%). With those forces this model's elbow torques move the wrong way, because its elbow placement and fixed shoulders don't match real pressing, so the default stays at zero. The shoulder joints stay put; real shoulder blades move, so the mid-press elbow numbers are probably on the high side.

variants.name: Incline bench (30°), medium grip
variants.notes: Bench tilted 30°: the bar touches the upper chest and presses vertically over the shoulders. Each hand pushes up with half the bar; how hard the hands pull the bar apart (or squeeze it) can't be found from statics, so by default they don't. Lifters do pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow, and the least-effort option predicts similar values (26%, 41%, 2%).
